title: Do men and women have different brains?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine whether men's and women's brains differ. They note that large longitudinal studies show cognitive ability and IQ differences are almost negligible, but structural and compositional brain differences exist. Topics include hypothalamus differences, the corpus callosum-free brain size discussion, gray matter versus white matter (men about six and a half times more gray matter, women about ten times more white matter), neuron density in women's cortex (Sandra Witelson's work at McMaster), a Yale phoneme-removal study using brain imaging where men and women performed equally but used different regions, the 2001 finding on frontal lobe and parietal cortex differences, nature versus nurture debate including Witelson's study of Einstein's brain, stereotype threat examples in math, and implications for drug testing, schizophrenia treatment, and physical therapy and brain injury. The episode closes with listener mail containing a jingle written for the show by Rusty Machia of Mighty Mas Media, plus calls to contact the show.
topics: brain structure differences between men and women

segments.title: Introduction and framing the debate
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the topic of whether men's and women's brains differ, noting the policy implications and that the field is still nascent. They mention Sandra Witelson's 1990s comparison of brains and that cognitive ability differences in longitudinal studies are small.

segments.title: Hypothalamus and brain size
segments.summary: The hosts discuss older ideas that sex differences were limited to the hypothalamus, which controls sex drive and food intake, and describe structural differences there such as the suprachiasmatic nucleus and androgen receptor patterns. They also note men's brains are on average somewhat larger after adjusting for body size, and that this does not equate to intelligence, tying back to a myths of the brain discussion about neuron ratios.

segments.title: Regional differences, gray and white matter
segments.summary: A 2001 finding showed that frontal lobe and orbitofrontal cortex are larger in women, while parietal cortex and amygdala are larger in men. Men have about six and a half times more gray matter, and women about ten times more white matter. The hosts speculate on how these differences relate to thinking styles and efficiency, and Witelson's finding that women have about twelve percent more neurons packed into some cortical regions linked to incoming and outgoing signals.

segments.title: Yale phoneme study and sense of direction
segments.summary: A Yale study from around the turn of the 1990s used brain imaging while participants removed phonemes from words such as Germany to Gurney. Men and women performed equally but men used a small region of one hemisphere while women used regions in both. The hosts find it striking since reading is a recent skill. Chuck shares his poor sense of direction and his wife Emily's better map reading.
topics: spatial orientation and sense of direction

segments.title: Nature versus nurture, math stereotypes, and practical implications
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether differences are innate or shaped by society, citing Molly Edmonds' point about gender-typed upbringing and Witelson's study of Einstein's brain as evidence of structural differences at birth. They describe brain plasticity and pruning, the stereotype threat studies involving female math students and white males told of Asian comparisons, and the practical implications for drug trials, schizophrenia treatment, physical therapy, and frontal lobe injury recovery.

segments.title: Closing thoughts on embracing differences
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck wrap up by saying the research should be studied to provide medical and therapy benefits and that brains are both different and trainable. They suggest the search bar on the site for the related article.
